passage: Dear Matthias, a letter instead of a call because this needs to be got right, and you know how I am on the telephone. The answer is yes: I will make your wedding suit, and it will be my last commission, and I want you to understand what that means so you carry it lightly rather than heavily. Fifty-two years of tailoring end with you, by my choice, and there is no better ending on offer; I measured your grandfather for his wedding in 1959, your father for his in 1987, and there is a line in my order book waiting for your name since, frankly, the day you were born. The cloth is already chosen, pending your veto: a gray worsted from the last bolt of the mill at Harnden before it closed, which I have hoarded for eleven years for a reason I could not have named until your letter came. Three fittings, no arguments: the first in March, muslin only, the second in May, and the last a fortnight before the day. Bring your Elsa to the second fitting; brides see what mirrors miss. Payment we will discuss once, briefly, and my price will be unreasonable in the direction that offends you, and you will accept it because the last suit is the tailor's to price. My hands are steady in the morning, so fittings are at nine. Yours, with the tape already around my neck, Old Verner.
question: From which mill's last bolt is the gray worsted cloth?

passage: Dear Dr. Osmund, a report from your least promising patient, twelve years on, which you may read aloud to whichever student is currently sitting in the corner chair losing hope. When you discharged me from the stroke ward you set three goals in the notes, which I obtained and have kept: stairs unaided, a return to the garden, and, marked doubtful in your own hand, the violin. I write to correct the record. Stairs came in the first year, as you predicted. The garden took four; the left hand would grip a trowel long before it would release one, which nobody warns you is the harder trick. The violin took eleven years, and I will not pretend the road was straight: I sold the instrument in year six in a black month, bought it back in year seven at a loss of 200 dollars and some pride, and hired, of all people, a teacher of beginners aged five to eight, Miss Adderley, who treated me exactly like her other pupils, star charts included, which was precisely the medicine. This spring I played in her end of year concert, programme enclosed, third item, between two eight-year-olds, one of whom I am pleased to say I outperformed. The doubtful is yours to keep; I have no further use for it. With respect and mischief, Konrad Weiss.
question: How many years did the violin take to come back?

passage: Dear Sigrid, you left your notebook on the train, and I am the stranger who has it, so let me begin with proof: page one is a list titled things I will not apologize for, and item four is reading the last chapter first. Your name and this address are inside the cover, which is the only page I read on purpose; the list I saw while checking, and I have thought about item four all week. The notebook is safe, dry, and unread beyond that page, wrapped in the brown paper my bookseller uses, and I will post it tomorrow, or, if you prefer and since the cover also says you take the 7:40 on weekdays, I can simply leave it with the guard at Ellsmere station, whom I have known twenty years and who holds things honestly. I confess a selfish motive for this letter beyond the logistics: I am a retired schoolteacher of English, and whoever writes lists with titles like yours should be writing more than lists, which is exactly the kind of unasked advice item seven, no unsolicited advice from strangers, forbids me to give, so consider it not given. The paper takes ink well, by the way; I tested one corner of the wrapping, not the notebook, with my good pen. Awaiting instructions, and I remain, respectfully, A. Pelham, carriage C, the window seat.
question: What is item four on the notebook's first list?

passage: Dear Tante Mirre, the restaurant survived its first winter, and since you loaned us the deposit when three banks would not, you get the numbers before anyone, including, please, before Uncle Jens, who will turn them into advice. We served 9,100 covers between October and March, which the spreadsheet calls 6 percent above plan, and the plan, you will remember, was written by two optimists at your kitchen table. The fish soup, your mother's recipe with our one change, outsold every other main two nights of three; the change stays secret, though you of all people could taste it in a spoonful. We lost the pastry chef in January to the hotel at Vosskamp, a blow, and rather than replace him at winter wages we shortened the dessert list to four things we do perfectly, and complaints, to our astonishment, went down. The freezer failed on the night of the December storm and Rikard drove the whole fish stock to the ice house at the harbor at two in the morning in the neighbor's van, which is now a story the staff tell applicants as a warning and I tell you as a boast. We can begin repaying in May, 400 a month to start. You will say keep it longer; we will not. The corner table is yours forever, and it has the view. Love from both of us, Sanne.
question: How many covers did the restaurant serve between October and March?

passage: Dear Grandfather, greetings from the research station, where it is minus 31 outside and your socks, the gray pair you knitted against all mockery, are on my feet inside two other pairs and outperforming equipment that cost the institute 200 dollars. I am writing by the generator's light at the end of my first month of winter-over, and I owe you the letter I promised at the airport, the one with no brave face in it. So: the dark is heavier than I expected, the loneliness is lighter, and the work is the best I have ever done. I mind the wind more than the cold and the quiet more than the wind, and on the worst day so far, when the storm pinned us in for 60 hours and the radio mast came down, it was, of all your sayings, the one about lambing season that got me up the ladder in the lull to splice the guy wire: the weather does not care how you feel, so feel it on the way. Dr. Halvorsen has made me deputy for the met readings, which means I am trusted with the 3 a.m. observation, and I have seen auroras that made the whole station stand in the snow in silence like a congregation. Nine months remain. Feed Bella her fish skins on Fridays; she will have told you otherwise. Your Ingrid.
question: For how many hours did the storm pin the station in?

passage: Dear Mr. Abernathy, I write concerning the hedge, and I ask you to notice, before anything else, that this letter is friendly, because the last three exchanges between our houses were conducted through solicitors, and my husband and I have concluded that the solicitors are the only parties enjoying themselves. The survey we jointly commissioned arrived Tuesday, as you know, and it says what neither of us hoped: the boundary runs not along the hedge but through it, 40 centimeters our side at the road and 60 centimeters your side at the shed, the hedge having wandered, as the surveyor put it with what I felt was inappropriate delight, like a river. We could litigate the river. The estimate for that road, from my own solicitor in an honest moment, begins at 4,000 dollars and ends nowhere. Or we could accept his other suggestion, made off the record: declare the hedge a joint possession, split the trimming as we split the survey fee, and plant the gap at the north end, where the hedge died in the drought year, together, this autumn, with whips at 2 dollars each from the nursery at Fallow Cross. My husband votes hawthorn. I vote beech. You, sir, hold the casting vote, and I can think of no cheaper way to end a war. Over the hedge, as it were, Prudence Malloy.
question: How far onto the writer's side does the boundary run at the road?

passage: Dear Felix, the observatory committee has counted the votes, and I get the pleasure of telling you, before the formal letter does, that the new telescope will be named the Hartmann, after your grandmother. The vote was not close: 61 of 74 members, on the first ballot, with the other candidates being a dead astronomer nobody local remembers and, inevitably, a proposal to sell the name to the highest bidder, which received two votes, both, we suspect, from the treasurer. I wish you had been in the room for the speeches. Old Fenn stood up with his notes shaking and told the story none of us knew in full: how in the winter of 1963 the society's first mirror, ordered at ruinous cost from abroad, arrived cracked, and how Greta Hartmann, then the society's secretary and its only member with optics training, declared she would regrind it herself, and did, over eleven months, in the cellar under the chemist's shop, checking the figure with a knife edge test she built from a razor blade and a bicycle lamp, and how the mirror she saved served this society for forty years and never once, Fenn said, showed us a false star. The dedication is set for the October open night. You will unveil the plaque, no arguments; you have her hands, the committee agreed, and it is the committee's telescope. Warmly, Ilona.
question: How many of the 74 members voted for the name Hartmann?

passage: Dear Ruthie, a letter from the road, as promised, one per country, and this is the third: we are in the mountains now, staying above the treeline in a hut that rents bunks to cyclists and judges them by their gears. The tandem is holding. The word for how the second climb went does not exist in polite letters, but the descent on the far side was 22 kilometers of switchbacks through cloud that opened once, theatrically, to show us the whole valley in evening light, and Deniz stopped pedaling and said, out loud, to the valley in general, we are the luckiest fools alive, and a sheep answered, and that is now the motto of the expedition. Practical matters: the rear wheel needed a new rim at Tolvan, 90 dollars and a day's wait, during which we were adopted by the mechanic's family, fed three times, and taught a card game whose rules changed, we are certain, whenever we began winning. Deniz's knee, which you asked about, behaves if we keep the cadence up and the pride down. We average 70 kilometers a day, less than planned, better than hoped. Next letter from the coast, where we intend to put the tandem on a boat and our feet in the sea in that order. Kiss the cat, water nothing, love everything. Your wandering sister, Amara.
question: How long was the descent on the far side of the second climb?

passage: Dear Mr. Tolliver, my father, Wim Deckers, asked me to write to you, and dictated the heart of this letter from his chair by the window, so the voice is his even where the handwriting is mine. He wishes you to know, first, that the chess games by post must end, after 26 years and, by his ledger, 214 games, because his eyes have finally overruled him; the specialist was kind, but the board swims, and he will not, he says, insult the game by guessing. He wishes you to know, second, the standing of the rivalry, which he has kept in the green notebook since the first game in 1999: 101 wins to you, 98 to him, 15 draws, and he requires me to state plainly that the unfinished game, where his knight stood proudly on e5, is to be recorded as abandoned, not resigned, and he trusts you to honor the distinction, as you honored the rules through a friendship in which, remarkably, you have met in person only twice. Third, and here he made me stop and steady the sentence: he says the Thursday envelopes were, for a quarter of a century, the fixed point of his week, and he does not know how to thank a man for that, so he sends instead the white queen from his own set, which he asks you to keep on your desk, promoted, as it were, to memory. My father hopes you will write still, without the moves. He remains, your opponent and friend, Wim. And I remain his hand, Katrien Deckers.
question: How many games did the two men play by post, by the father's ledger?

passage: Dear Planning Committee, I am eleven years old and I am writing about the pond on Whitlow Common because my father says the committee reads every letter, and I am testing this. You are deciding whether to fill the pond for the new path. I am against it, and I am writing with my reasons, which are not the reasons in the petition, because I signed that too and you already have it. Reason one: I have counted the newts every spring for four years for the wildlife club, with Miss Devi checking my numbers, and this year I counted 34, which is eleven more than my first year, and the count sheets are in the club records at the library if you do not believe a child, which item 6 of your own charter says you must not do, I looked it up. Reason two: the path can go around the pond, and I have drawn a map on the back of this letter showing how, and measured it with the trundle wheel from school, and the long way is only 90 meters longer, which is 120 steps, I counted twice. Reason three is not a number: my grandmother taught me to skim stones there, and she is gone now, and the pond still has her in it a bit, which I cannot prove like the newts, but it is true anyway. Please come and see it in April when the newts are busy. I will show you where to stand. Yours faithfully, Tobias Wren, junior member, Whitlow Wildlife Club.
question: How many newts did the writer count this year?
